title: Beef Rendang
subtitle: Slow-cooked dry Indonesian beef curry
excerpt: The most celebrated dish of the Minangkabau people of West Sumatra: beef cooked very slowly in spiced coconut milk until all the liquid has evaporated and the beef fries in its own coconut fat, developing a dark, crumbly, intensely aromatic crust.

recipe.sourceNotes: Rendang is a slow-cooked dry curry originating from the Minangkabau highlands of West Sumatra, Indonesia, and is one of the few dry meat curries in South-East Asian cooking. The technique involves cooking beef in coconut milk with a spice paste (rempah) over several hours until all the liquid has been absorbed and evaporated, at which point the coconut fat separates out and the beef literally fries in coconut oil, developing the characteristic dark, caramelised exterior. In its driest form (rendang kering) it can be kept without refrigeration for several weeks due to the antimicrobial properties of the spices and dry coconut. A wet rendang (kalio) is an earlier stage of cooking when some sauce remains. The spice paste typically includes galangal, lemongrass, turmeric leaf, kaffir lime leaves, and a complex dried chilli blend.

content.text: The long, very low heat cook requires patience and attention in the final phase when the coconut milk has reduced and the beef is frying; stir frequently to prevent burning. The beef should be cut into large chunks and will pull apart into pieces as it cooks. Galangal (a fragrant rhizome related to ginger but distinct in flavour) is available from Asian supermarkets and is essential; ginger is not a substitute.

content.text: Blend the chillies, shallots, garlic, and ginger to a smooth paste. Toast the desiccated coconut in a dry pan until golden; pound or blend to a paste (kerisik) and set aside.

Combine the beef, coconut milk, blended paste, lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, turmeric, salt, and sugar in a large, heavy pan. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 2 to 3 hours, stirring occasionally, until the liquid has mostly evaporated.

Once the liquid has gone and the beef is frying in coconut fat, stir constantly over medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes until the beef is dark and deeply caramelised. Stir in the kerisik. Taste and season. Serve with steamed jasmine rice.
